How to Actually Remember What You Study: 5 Science-Backed Methods

Amaka Okafor · Published Sep 12, 2026 · 7 min read

Last updated September 18, 2026

If you've ever finished re-reading a chapter and felt confident, only to blank out on the exam, you're not alone — and it's not a sign you have a bad memory. It usually means you used a study method that feels effective but isn't. Cognitive scientists have spent decades testing which techniques actually build durable memory, and the results consistently point to a small set of methods that most students never learn in school. Here are five of them, and how to put each one into practice this week.

Why re-reading feels productive but isn't

Re-reading your notes creates something psychologists call fluency — the material starts to feel familiar, and that familiarity gets mistaken for understanding. The problem is that fluency fades fast under exam pressure, because you were never actually forced to retrieve the information from memory; you were just recognizing it on the page in front of you.

The techniques below work because they replace passive review with effortful retrieval — the same mental action you'll need to perform on exam day.

1. Use spaced repetition

Instead of studying a topic once for three hours, study it for 30 minutes today, 20 minutes in three days, and 15 minutes a week later. Each time you almost forget the material and then recall it, the memory gets stronger and the next forgetting curve gets flatter.

Try this
After every study session, write tomorrow's date and next week's date in your planner with a note of exactly what to review. Apps like Anki automate this schedule for you using flashcards.

2. Practice active recall

Close the textbook and try to write down everything you remember about a topic before checking your notes. Getting an answer wrong during practice is not wasted effort — the act of struggling to retrieve information, even unsuccessfully, strengthens the memory pathway more than passively re-reading the correct answer would have.

  • Turn each heading in your notes into a question, then answer it from memory
  • Use past exam questions as your primary study material, not a final check
  • Cover your notes and try to reconstruct a diagram or process from scratch

3. Mix topics with interleaving

Studying one topic for a long block (called "blocking") feels organized, but switching between related topics in the same session — called interleaving — forces your brain to actively choose which method or formula applies, which mirrors what an exam actually demands. If you're revising math, alternate between problem types rather than doing twenty of the same kind in a row.

A quick example

Instead of solving ten quadratic equations back to back, mix in a few linear equations and word problems between them. It will feel harder in the moment — that difficulty is the sign it's working.

4. Explain it to someone else

If you can't explain a concept in plain language to a younger sibling or a friend outside the subject, you likely don't understand it as well as you think. This is sometimes called the Feynman Technique — teaching exposes the exact gaps that re-reading conceals.

"If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough." — a principle widely attributed to Richard Feynman

5. Protect your sleep before the exam

Memory consolidation — the process of moving information from short-term to long-term storage — happens largely during sleep. Sacrificing sleep for a few extra hours of cramming often backfires, because the material you crammed never gets consolidated properly. Aim for consistent sleep in the final week before an exam rather than pulling an all-nighter beforehand.

Frequently asked questions

What is the most effective way to memorize study material?

Active recall combined with spaced repetition is the most effective, research-backed combination. Testing yourself on material at increasing intervals strengthens memory far more than passive re-reading. Studies show that retrieval practice improves long-term retention by 50-100% compared to study methods like highlighting or re-reading.

How long before an exam should I start studying?

Ideally 3 to 4 weeks, so spaced repetition has room to work. Cramming in the final 1 to 2 days can still help with short-term recall, but it does not build the durable memory that spacing does. Research by cognitive psychologist Harry Bahrick shows spacing improves retention by up to 80% over massed practice.

Does re-reading notes help you remember them?

Re-reading creates a false sense of familiarity but is one of the least effective study methods. Actively testing yourself on the material produces significantly better long-term retention. A meta-analysis of learning techniques ranked re-reading as one of the lowest-utility strategies, while retrieval practice and interleaving ranked among the highest.

What is the Feynman Technique and how does it help studying?

The Feynman Technique is a learning method where you explain a concept in plain language to someone unfamiliar with the topic. This exposes gaps in your understanding that passive re-reading would miss. Named after physicist Richard Feynman, it forces active retrieval and makes complex ideas simpler, both of which strengthen memory.

How does sleep affect exam performance and memory?

Memory consolidation — the process of moving information from short-term to long-term storage — happens largely during sleep. Sacrificing sleep for extra study hours often backfires because cramped information never consolidates properly. Aim for 7-9 hours consistently in the week before an exam rather than pulling all-nighters.
